title: The hedge around Job; the wife’s counsel and Eve’s pattern
english: “Have you not fenced round what is outside him?” (Job 1:10). How do you know that it has been fenced? This is our adversary the devil, who goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to swallow (1 Peter 5:8). So he came round Job too, wanting to do the same things to him. Later, once he had received authority, he did them. That everything was fenced round he understood from the very fact that he had been held back; and since he wanted to do his work on Job, he said: “You have fenced round what is inside him and what is outside him.” Everything, then, so far as it is not handed over to the devil, you have fenced round.

“While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said to Job: While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking at the house of their elder brother, suddenly a great wind came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell on your children, and they died. I alone escaped, and I have come to tell you” (Job 1:18-19). The camels, then, he made fall to the horsemen, and the donkeys and the yokes of oxen to the raiders; but the sheep he hated, and that is why he brought fire down on them. He laid a plot against the sons as well, and kept looking for a moment to destroy them. If he had found them reading, he would not have touched the house, nor would he have had any opening to kill them. If he had found them praying, he could have done nothing against them. But when he found his opportunity, he prevailed. What, then, was the opportunity? There was drunkenness; there was a drinking party. Notice the words “the wind struck the corners of the house”: it is in the broad places of the corners that the hypocrites stand and pray (Matthew 6:5), and everyone who has not set foot on the straight road makes use of corners. A broad corner is wickedness that is great and unbridled.

“And the Lord said to the devil: Where do you come from?” (Job 2:2). God saw how Satan, put to shame, was in torment. And whenever, on questioning someone, God sees him acting without good sense, then he convicts the evildoer, as he convicted Cain.

“When time had gone on, his wife said to him” (Job 2:9). See the villainy. When a long time had gone by, that is when he attacks; for that is when strength is at its weakest. The weakness was twofold: the man bearing the trials had grown weaker through the length of time, and his hope had been given up all the more.

And a little later: Let us not, then, look at the fact that she is his wife, but at what she advises. This I urge on people today as well: do not look at the rank of the persons, but at the kind of counsel they give. A wife exists to help, not to trip up.

“His wife said to him: How long will you hold out?” (Job 2:9). The device stronger than all the devices before it, the devil brings up last. Would that you had taken her too! Would that you had buried her with the children! Some say that the words were not even the woman's, but that he himself, having shaped himself into her, was uttering them; for it was not possible for Job's wife to be such a woman, unless one were to say that she became such after being overturned by calamity.

And a little later: It is likely that this was not the first time this counsel had been given, but that he had often heard many things harsher than these from his wife. See the devilish deceit. He thought of Eve. “This,” he says, “brought down the first man; this will be able to get the better of this man too.” But, you wretched and senseless one! She found that man weaker than his belly and sowed her own venom; but this man you see living as a philosopher and mastering nature itself. The loss of his goods did not bend him, nor the untimely death of his children, nor the comfortless torture of his body, nor so long a stretch of time. The man whom events did not capture, do you expect to subdue with words?
From the same: Why do you unnerve the athlete? Why do you pull down his hands? You ought to have said, as the Apostle does: “Yet a little while, yet a little while” (Hebrews 10:37).
